parole.significato: battle axe (axe for use in battle)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese acha, from Old French hache (“battle-axe”), from Frankish.
Borrowed from Old French douelle, diminutive of douve / doue, from Latin doga (“vessel”). Compare Galician doela, Spanish duela.

From the Old French adjective ancestrel, from the noun ancestre (“ancestor”), from Late Latin antecessor (“predecessor”), an agent noun from the past participle stem of Latin antecedere (“to proceed”), from the prefix ante- with the infinitive cedere (“to go”), the former from Proto-Italic *kezdō (“
From Old Galician-Portuguese ãcião, borrowed from Old French ancien, from Vulgar Latin *anteānus.
From Old French antelop, from Medieval Latin antilops, from Byzantine Greek ἀνθόλοψ (anthólops).

parole.significato: apprentice (a trainee, especially in a skilled trade)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French aprentis, with spelling influenced by aprender. First attested in c. 15th century.

parole.significato: a full suit of armour, coat of mail
parole.testo: From Old French herneis or hernois.

parole.significato: grappling, grapple (tool with claws or hooks)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French harpeau. By surface analysis, arpão + -éu.
From Old French arrumer. Compare with arrimar. Perhaps from Proto-Celtic *ad-φrima-Ø.
Borrowed from Old French azimut, from Arabic اَلسَّمْت (as-samt, “the direction”).

parole.significato: bachelor (someone who has achieved a bachelor’s degree)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bachiller, from Old French bacheler, from Medieval Latin baccalaureus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese banir (att. 1371), from Old French banir, from Late Latin bannīre, from Frankish.

parole.significato: haggle (to argue for a better deal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French bargaigner (“to bargain”). Compare French barguigner and English bargain.
From Old French baron. Doublet of varão.
From Old Galician-Portuguese bastardo, from Old French bastard, from Late Latin bastardus, from Frankish.
From Old Galician-Portuguese bastir, borrowed from Old French bastir (“to build”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese batel, from Old French batel (“boat”) (Modern French bateau).

parole.significato: trunk, chest (a large strong, usually wooden, box with a secure convex lid)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese baul, from Old French bahur (Modern French bahut).
Borrowed from Old French bedel.
From Old French bossel, diminutive of boce (“knob-like swelling”).

parole.significato: float (buoyant device used to support something in water)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French buie, boye, boue, from Frankish *baukn.

parole.significato: baldric (strap made of leather or other material, worn by soldiers to suspend their weapon or to secure the staff of a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French baldré. Compare modern French baudrier. Doublet of baldréu and bálteo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese botar, from Old French bouter (“to strike, push”), from Frankish *bautan (“to push, strike, beat”), from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to beat”).

parole.significato: rowing boat (boat propelled only by oars)
parole.testo: From Old French bot, from Middle English bot, from Old English bāt.

parole.significato: wad (soft seal used in shotgun cartridges and cannons)
parole.testo: Uncertain, possibly from Old French bousche.

parole.significato: pocketknife, penknife (small razor with one or more blades and other movable and retractable accessories, which fit int…
parole.testo: From to Old French canivet, cnivet (“little knife”), from Frankish *knīf (“knife”), from Proto-Germanic *knībaz (“knife”), from *knīpaną (“to pinch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gneybʰ-. Compare French canif.

From Old Galician-Portuguese carcaix, from Old French carquais, from Byzantine Greek ταρκάσιον (tarkásion), from Arabic تَرْكَاش (tarkāš), from Persian ترکش (tarkaš), from earlier تیرکش (tirkaš, “quiver; arrowslit”), from تیر (tir, “arrow”) + کش (kaš, “container”).
Borrowed from Old French chanfreindre.

Borrowed from Old French chapel, from Early Medieval Latin cappellus, from Late Latin cappa. Doublet of capelo. Compare Galician chapeu, Spanish chapeo, chapeau, Catalan capell, Occitan capèl, French chapeau, and Italian cappello (the Galician and Spanish also being borrowings from French).
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Old French chalemel (French chalumeau), from Latin calamus (“reed”).

parole.significato: chisel (tool consisting of an oblong piece of metal ending in a sharp edge)
parole.testo: From older cisel (influenced by pincel "paintbrush"), from Old French cisel, from cisoir (with a change in suffix), from Late Latin cīsōrium (“cutting instrument”), ultimately from Latin caedere (“cut”).

parole.significato: swan (any of various species of large, long-necked waterfowl, of genus Cygnus)
parole.testo: From Old French cisne, from Late Latin cicinus, from Latin cycnus, ultimately from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos, “swan”).
Borrowed from Old French conestable, influenced by conde (“count”), from Late Latin comes stabulī (“officer of the stables”).
Based on Old French condoléance. Compare also Spanish condolencia.
From Old French cotte, from Latin cotta (“undercoat, tunic”), see also German Kutte.

From Old Galician-Portuguese covardia, from covarda, from Old French coart, cuard, from coe (“tail”) + -ard (“pejorative agent noun”); coe is in turn from Latin cauda. The reference seems to be to an animal “turning tail”, or having its tail between its legs, especially a dog.

Alteration of esmaiar, from Old French esmaier, from Vulgar Latin *exmagāre (“lose the strength”), from Frankish *magan (“to have strength”). Compare Galician desmaiar, Spanish desmayar and Spanish esmayar

parole.significato: to disassemble (to undo something piece by piece)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French desmancher (“to remove a tool’s handle”), from des- (“un-; dis-”) + manche (“handle”) + -ar. Cognate with French démancher.
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], borrowed from Old French despechier (compare modern dépêcher).
From Old French desport, variant of deport (“enjoyment, fun”), from Latin deportāre (“to bring”). Doublet of deportar, desporte, and esporte.
Borrowed from Old French deien, from Latin decānus. Doublet of decano.
From Old Galician-Portuguese duc (“duke”), borrowed from Old French duc (“duke”), from Latin dux (“ruler”), from dūcō (“to lead”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk-. Doublet of doge.
Borrowed from Old French empeechier, from Latin impedicāre (“to fetter”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese engendrar (14th c.), from Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerāre. Compare Old Galician-Portuguese engerar (inherited from Latin) and modern gerar < generāre.

parole.significato: to prop (support or shore up something)
parole.testo: From escora (“nautical list”) + -ar, from Old French score, from Dutch schoor.
From Old French esgart (“look”) (French égard).

Possibly through the intermediate of Old French esmeralde (Modern French émeraude), from Vulgar Latin *smeralda, *smaraldus, alteration of Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), of Semitic origin.

parole.significato: stay (a strong rope or wire supporting a mast)
parole.testo: From Old French estai (Modern French étai), from Old English stæġ (“rope, stay”), from Proto-Germanic *stagą.

parole.significato: yardstick, standard (something used as a measure for comparative evaluations)
parole.testo: From Old French estalon (“stallion”), current French étalon (“standard”).

parole.significato: badge of a religious, military or civil corporation
parole.testo: From Old French estandart. Cognate with English standard. Doublet of estândar, via English.
Probably borrowed from Old French estrikier (“to make longer, to stretch”); ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan (“to stretch”). Compare Galician estricar.
From Old French estioler, modern French étioler (“to make pale”). Compare English etiolate.

parole.significato: to wound with a tuck or rapier
parole.testo: From estoque (“rapier”) + -ar, from Old French estoc.
Borrowed from Old French estoc.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese strangeiro, borrowed from Old French estrangier. Compare Galician estranxeiro, Modern French étranger.
Borrowed from Old French farse, French farce.
Relatinization of earlier frecha (influenced by French flèche), from Old Galician-Portuguese frecha, from Old French fleche, from Vulgar Latin *fleccia, from Frankish *fliukkijā.
From Old Galician-Portuguese folia, in turn from Old French folie. Cognate with Galician folía.
From fornir + -ecer, from Old French fornir.
Borrowed from Old French feurre, from Frankish *fodar, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą, from Proto-Indo-European *pātróm (“food”).

parole.significato: to frown (to form wrinkles in forehead)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Old French froncir (“to wrinkle, frown”), from Frankish *hrunkja "a wrinkle" from Proto-Germanic *hrunkijō, *hrunkitō (“fold, wrinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). Less likely from Latin frangere; cf. however also franger.
Borrowed from Old French galilée, from Medieval Latin galilaea, from Latin Galilaea (“Galilee”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese galee, a borrowing from Old French galee, from Byzantine Greek γάλεα (gálea), from γαλέη (galéē, “type of shellfish”), from Ancient Greek γαλεός (galeós, “shark”).

parole.significato: hinge (device for the pivoting of a door)
parole.testo: From Old French gons, from Latin gomphus, from Ancient Greek γόμφος (gómphos), from Proto-Hellenic *gómpʰos, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese grangia, from Old French grange (“barn”), from Vulgar Latin *grānica (“grain storage barn, granary; grange, small farm”), from Latin grānum (“grain”) from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Cognate with Galician granxa and Spanish granja.

parole.significato: a grill used for barbecuing food
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French greille, from Latin craticula. Doublet of the inherited gradelha, and of the neological borrowing cratícula.
Borrowed from Old French greve (“greave”).

parole.significato: grey / gray (having a colour between white and black)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese gris, from Old French gris, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz (“grey”).
From Old French guion (“script”) + -ista.
Borrowed from Old French jaiole, from Late Latin caveola, from Latin cavea (“cage”) + -ola (diminutive ending). Compare gaiola, an inherited doublet, and Spanish jaula, likewise borrowed from French.

parole.significato: javelin (throwing spear used as a weapon)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French javeline, diminutive of javelot, from Celtic *gablakko-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese joya, from Old French joie (modern joyau), from Vulgar Latin *jocale, from Latin jocus. Compare Catalan joia and Spanish joya.
From Old French laton, from Arabic لَاطُون (lāṭūn, “copper, copper alloy”), from Proto-Common Turkic *altun (“gold”). Compare Karakhanid اَلْتُونْ (altūn, “gold”).
Possibly borrowed from Old French lier, from Latin ligāre. Doublet of ligar and legar.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ligeyro, borrowed from Old French legier, from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from Latin *levius (“light”) + -ārius (adjective-forming suffix). Cognate with Fala ligeru, Galician lixeiro, Spanish ligero. Piecewise doublet of leveiro.

parole.significato: lineage (series or succession of ancestors or descendants)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese linhagem, from Old French lignage.
From Old French liois, modern French liais.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese logea (“storehouse”). Sense 3 is a semantic loan from French loge.

parole.significato: only used in de lés a lés
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French lez, from Latin latus. Doublet of lado.
Borrowed from Old French mainel, from Latin manuālis (“suitable to be hand-held”).
Borrowed from Old French mastin.

From mensagem (“message”) + -eiro (“-eer”) (compare Galician mensaxeiro, Spanish mensajero), from Old French message (“message”), from Late Latin missāticum, from Latin missum, the supine of mittō (“to send”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”).
Borrowed from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missaticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese montar, from Old French monter, from Vulgar Latin *mōntāre, from Latin montem (“mountain”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Old French morne (“gloomy”). Compare Galician morno.
Borrowed from Old French moustarde, from moust (“must”), from Latin mustum.
From Old French nivel, livel, from Vulgar Latin *libellus, from Latin lībella, from lībra.

parole.significato: shroud (thick cable headed on a ship's mast, which serves as lateral support)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French hobenc /hobent, from Old Norse höfuðbendur. Compare French hauban.
From Old French panel, from Latin pannus. Compare English panel.
From Old Galician-Portuguese paje, from Old French page.

parole.significato: a fried pastry made of wheat flour, filled with cheese, meat or other fillings; comparable to German Teigtaschen
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French pastel (modern pâte).

parole.significato: toll (fee for using roads and bridges)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French portage.
Borrowed from Old French portatil, from Medieval Latin portātilis, from portātus. Noun senses are semantic loans from English portable.
From Old French platel (French plateau (“tray”)).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese prison, borrowed from Old French prison, from Latin prehēnsiō, from prehendō (“to seize”) + -tiō. Doublet of preensão.
From Old Galician-Portuguese proeza, from Old French proece, proeche, proesce (compare modern French prouesse) or Old Occitan proeza.
From Old Galician-Portuguese quite, from Old French quitte (“free; liberated”), from Latin quiētus. Doublet of quieto and quedo.
From Old French rebec, from Arabic رَبَاب (rabāb). Doublet of arrabil and arrabel.
From Old French ralée.
From Old French rechacier, from chacier (modern chasser), from Vulgar Latin *captiāre, whence also Portuguese caçar. Compare Spanish rechazar.
Borrowed from Old French rondon.
Borrowed from Old French roc.
Borrowed from Old French rote (modern French route).
From Old French rote, from Germanic.

From Old Galician-Portuguese rua (“street”), from or influenced by Old French rue (Modern French rue) or Old Spanish rua (Modern Spanish rúa), from Vulgar Latin *ruga (“furrow, path, street”), from Latin ruga (“wrinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *krewp- (“to become encrusted”). Cognate with Galicia

parole.significato: rhubarb (any plant of the genus Rheum)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French reubarbe, from Late Latin reubarbarum, probably from Koine Greek ῥῆον βαρβαρικόν (rhêon barbarikón), from Ancient Greek ῥῆον (rhêon, “rhubarb”) + βαρβαρικόν (barbarikón), neuter of βαρβαρικός (barbarikós, “foreign; barbaric”).
Borrowed from Old French res (modern rez). Doublet of raso.

parole.significato: to sail; to cross the seas
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese singrar, from Old French singler (“to sail”), from Old Norse segl (“sail”), from Proto-Germanic *seglą (“sail”).

Borrowed from Old French talant, alternative form of talent, from Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money”), from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance; a particular weight, especially of gold; sum of money; a talent”). Doublet of talento.

parole.significato: torch (stick with a flame on one end)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tocha, from Old French torche, from Vulgar Latin *torca, from Late Latin torqua, from Latin torques.

parole.significato: tun (a large wooden barrel, a vat, a cask)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese tonel, from Old French tonel, from tone + -el (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from Late Latin tunna (“tun”), from Proto-Celtic *tunna (“hide, skin”). Doublet of tonelada. Cognate with Galician and Spanish tonel and Catalan tona.

parole.significato: metric ton, a unit of mass equal to 1000 kg
parole.testo: From tonel (“tun”) + -ada (“-ful”), from Old Galician-Portuguese tonel, from Old French tonel (“little tun, cask”), from tone + -el (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from Late Latin tunna (“tun”), from Proto-Celtic *tunna (“hide, skin”). In reference to the English unit, calqued from English ton. Doub
Borrowed from Old French top.

parole.significato: outrage (an offensive, immoral or indecent act)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French oltrage.
From Old French vague, from Old Norse vágr (“sea”), from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz (“wave, storm”).
